cards.title: Unit economics first: profit per order before anything else
cards.summary: Break down a single order's price, costs and gross margin before evaluating growth or marketing spend.
cards.use_when: You are launching or auditing a subscription box or physical product and need to know whether the business can make money per order before scaling ads.
steps: Write down the average order value (AOV). In the source case study, the subscription box was priced at $39/month with shipping baked in because customers expect free shipping — you mark up the price to absorb shipping rather than charging for it separately.
List every cost for one order: product cost (source example: $8.64), fulfillment/pick-and-pack at a third-party warehouse ($4.50), and shipping ($0.30) — total COGS $20.39.
Subtract COGS from AOV to get gross profit per order ($18.61 in the example).
Divide gross profit by AOV to get gross profit margin — 48% in the example.
The source is emphatic: if you don't know how much you make on one order, stop everything and figure it out first.
Keep this margin figure with you — you will multiply every lifetime revenue number by it to convert revenue into profit-based LTV.
caveats: Costs are illustrative, not benchmarks; substitute your own quotes for fulfillment and shipping.
Fulfillment and shipping are separate vendors in the source's example — do not conflate them.

cards.title: Use churn-rate lifetime as a fast fallback, not the real answer
cards.summary: A quick LTV approximation from churn rate and gross profit per order, useful only when you have no cohort data.
cards.use_when: You have a new subscription store with almost no retention history and need a rough LTV for early ad spend decisions.
steps: Estimate monthly churn rate: the percent of subscribers who cancel each month. Source case: 27%.
Compute average customer lifetime as 1 / churn rate. At 27% churn that is 3.7 months.
Multiply gross profit per order by the average lifetime to get LTV. $18.61 × 3.7 = $69 of gross profit per customer.
Use this number as a ceiling on marketing spend to acquire one new customer.

Treat it as a placeholder: the source says churn rate doesn't capture customer lifetime well because cancellation is front-loaded (see Dollar Shave Club: roughly 25% took off in the first month, but only about 10% churned across the entire second year).
Switch to cohort retention as soon as you have enough data — the source says once a company has more than a couple of people, retention cohorts are the way to think about it.
caveats: Assumes a roughly constant churn rate; real retention varies by how long the customer has been subscribed.
Source calls this a 'lazy' calculation to use only when you have nothing better.

cards.title: Read a retention cohort table to calculate lifetime revenue
cards.summary: Organize repeat purchases by signup month to see true retention, cumulative revenue and profit-based LTV over time.
cards.use_when: You have several months of subscription or repeat-purchase data and need a defensible customer lifetime value for ad budget decisions.
steps: Sort customers into cohorts by their first purchase month; label that month zero and each subsequent month 1, 2, 3…

Populate each cohort row with the number (or percentage) of that original group who purchase in each later month. Example: 100 bought in January, 81 came back in month one, 75 in month two, 45 in month three.
Divide each month's count by the starting month's count to express retention as a percentage.
Add a cumulative revenue row: sum each month's revenue from that cohort. The January cohort generated $3,750 in month zero and nearly $12,000 cumulatively by month three.
Divide cumulative revenue by the original cohort size to get lifetime revenue per customer ($116 in the example).

Multiply lifetime revenue by the gross profit margin (48%) to convert it into profit-based LTV — source example showed LTV building from about $18 in month one to $33, $47 and $55 over the next months.
Repeat each month as new data arrives; the curve tells you when LTV stops meaningfully increasing.
caveats: Works for non-subscription stores too — just read repeat purchases of the same cohort over time, as the source notes for gift-buying businesses.
Churn rate and cohort churn will disagree; the cohort view is more accurate because cancellation varies across the customer lifecycle.

cards.title: Blended vs paid CAC: calculate both and know why
cards.summary: Split acquisition cost into blended (all spend / all new customers) and paid-only (ad spend / paid-attributed new customers) to judge whether growth is scalable.
cards.use_when: You run paid ads plus organic channels and need to decide whether you can profitably increase ad budget.
steps: Collect monthly ad spend, total new customers, and the split of new customers attributed to paid vs non-paid channels using Google Analytics, Google Ads and Facebook Ads Manager.
Compute blended CAC: total ad spend ÷ total new customers. Source example: $6,500 ÷ 134 = $48.51 per new customer.
Compute paid CAC: ad spend ÷ paid-attributed new customers. Source example: $6,500 ÷ 101 = $64.
Always exclude returning customers from the denominator — including them produces a meaningless CAC, since CAC is about acquiring the first purchase.
Compare paid CAC to LTV ($69 in the example — yes, profitable, but 'barely').
Ask whether organic traffic is scalable; the source notes paid channels can scale from $500/day to $20,000/day quickly, while organic often cannot — so paid CAC is the number that constrains growth.
caveats: Channel splits require tracking setup; not every store will have it.
Blended CAC flatters performance when a large share of new customers come from non-scalable organic sources such as friends and family.

cards.title: Interpret the LTV:CAC ratio with the source's heuristics
cards.summary: Ratio of lifetime gross profit to acquisition cost signals whether the store can self-fund growth or needs outside capital.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to raise ad spend aggressively, seek investment, or fix retention/COGS first.
steps: Divide LTV by CAC. Source example: $69 LTV ÷ $48.50 blended CAC = 1.4.

Read the ratio against the source's stated bands: 1.0 is the bare minimum (you make no money before operating expenses); 2–3 is the target for growing profitably; mature SaaS businesses can see up to 6 because their lifetimes span many years.
If the ratio is low, the source's framing is that you will lose money on the early orders of each customer and need investment to bridge until customers become profitable.
If LTV is much higher than CAC, the source says the business can raise venture capital comparatively easily — investors are judging product stickiness and whether marketing scales without CAC rising.
Remember the ratio is based on gross profit only; payroll, fixed costs and other opex come out afterward.
caveats: The 2–3 and 'SaaS up to 6' figures are the presenter's heuristics, not universal benchmarks.
Ratio depends on which CAC you use (blended was 1.4 vs paid 1.4/1.4 — recalculate with paid CAC for a stricter view).

cards.title: Lever 1: Raise LTV by cutting churn and adding pause options
cards.summary: Small reductions in monthly churn have the largest single effect on lifetime value for subscription stores.
cards.use_when: Your LTV:CAC ratio is thin and you are looking for the highest-leverage place to improve subscription economics.
steps: Quantify the effect first using the churn shortcut: reducing churn from 27% to 20% raised LTV from $69 to $93 — a 35% increase in the source model.

Before cancellation, offer to pause or switch cadence: customers often cancel because they haven't finished the current box; letting them skip a month or take the box every other month keeps them subscribed.
Build email marketing that reminds, delights and drives repeat purchases, and invest in unusually responsive customer service to catch cancellations in the moment.
Requires automation — the source stresses you must respond fast enough to intercept the cancel intent.
Track retention at cohort level so you can see whether a pause option improves months 2–3 rather than just delaying churn.
caveats: The 27%→20% figures are from the source's illustrative model, not a predicted result for your store.
Pause options can mask churn rather than prevent it; watch whether customers resume or drift away.

cards.title: Lever 2: Raise AOV without competing on price
cards.summary: Upsells, tiers and value-based branding raise revenue per order and improve LTV.
cards.use_when: You want to raise LTV per subscriber without finding entirely new customers.
steps: Introduce tiers or upsells — e.g., a basic box at $39 and a premium box at $49 with more items. Higher revenue per order flows straight into lifetime value.
Build brand loyalty deliberately: the source argues customers who love the brand become less price-sensitive, which gives you pricing power.
Avoid competing on price — customers who buy because you are cheap focus on price, and the source notes they may keep buying a product they dislike for the price alone.
Combine with retention work: the same loyalty that supports price increases also reduces churn, compounding LTV from both directions.
Recalculate LTV after any tier change, since the mix shift alters both AOV and retention.
caveats: The source's tier prices are examples, not targets for your catalogue.
Price increases can damage retention if the perceived value does not justify them.

cards.title: Lever 3: Renegotiate COGS as volume grows
cards.summary: Product, fulfillment and shipping costs all fall with scale, increasing LTV without changing price or retention.
cards.use_when: You have grown order volume and want to convert scale into higher lifetime value and contribution margin.
steps: Decompose COGS into product cost, fulfillment and shipping, as in the source's $8.64 / $4.50 / $0.30 breakdown.
At low volume (source example: ~50 orders/month) you get the worst pricing — small production batches and small-volume fulfillment contracts.
At thousands of orders per month, buy product in larger wholesale quantities (the source models product cost dropping to about $7) and renegotiate the fulfillment contract (to about $4 per order).
Negotiate shipping rates as well — the source models shipping falling to about $6.50 in that line item, and notes every COGS line can be negotiated down.
Rerun your LTV model after renegotiation: in the source's illustration the combined reductions lifted LTV from $69 to about $80.
Attack LTV from every front simultaneously — retention, AOV and COGS — and keep re-checking it.
caveats: The renegotiated figures are illustrative model inputs, not quotes you should expect.
Some volume thresholds may be needed before suppliers or 3PLs will reprice.

cards.title: Decide how long a window to use for LTV
cards.summary: Choose an observation window by finding the point where cumulative cohort revenue stops meaningfully increasing.
cards.use_when: You need to fix a defensible LTV horizon for budgeting or investor conversations, especially for non-subscription or seasonal stores.
steps: Build a simple model: start with a cohort (e.g., 1,000 customers), apply a monthly churn rate (e.g., 25%), and track remaining customers month by month.
Multiply monthly remaining customers by AOV and accumulate into a running cumulative revenue total.
Extend the model month by month and watch where additional months add negligible revenue — the source's example stopped around month 12.
Use the cumulative total at that plateau as your customer lifetime revenue, then multiply by gross profit margin for LTV.

For non-subscription stores, build the same view as a cohort: how many people bought in a given month, and how their repeat purchases accumulate over time; the source still recommends a longer window than a first-purchase-only view.

For seasonal gift-buying stores (Mother's Day, Christmas), the source warns LTV is not limited to the first 60–90 days — a customer acquired once may return across holidays for years, so model a multi-year window.
caveats: A 60–90 day LTV view understates businesses with long repurchase cycles; the source explicitly calls this out for gift products.
The plateau month depends entirely on your retention curve — there is no universal window.

cards.title: Amazon launch: buy reviews with paid ads, harvest organic profit later
cards.summary: FBA product launches accept break-even or loss-making paid sales to accumulate reviews and climb organic rankings.
cards.use_when: You are launching a physical product on Amazon and deciding how much to lose on early ad-driven sales.
steps: Work out unit economics for the FBA product first: revenue per unit minus Amazon FBA fees (source example: about 20–25% of revenue, modeled at $20.56) minus landed product cost to Amazon (modeled at $25.30), leaving about $43.14 gross profit per order in the example.
Model paid acquisition: cost per click (source research example: $3.10) divided by conversion rate (7.5% in the example) gives cost per acquisition of about $41 per order.
Accept a thin or negative margin on paid orders — in the source example only $1.81 of profit per paid order — because the purpose is reviews, not first-order profit.
Target a review count before expecting organic lift; the source cites one founder aiming for about 100 reviews.
Shift to organic sales for actual profit: once ranked, customers find and buy without ad spend.

Attribution note: Amazon's site-wide conversion is reported around 10%, far above a typical store's 2–3%, because shopper intent is high — verify current conversion and CPC rates for your category rather than reusing these numbers.
caveats: CPC and conversion figures vary widely by niche; the source says conversion can range from 2–4% up to 30% depending on the product.
Conversion rates and ad platforms change often — verify the current Amazon Ads interface and category data.

cards.title: Model lifetime orders per customer before committing ad budget
cards.summary: Estimate how many times a customer repurchases to convert first-order profit into true lifetime value.
cards.use_when: You sell a consumable product and need to justify acquisition spend above first-order margin.
steps: Estimate average repurchase count from your own data — the source suggests looking across emails or an existing sales platform; the example used 2.2 lifetime purchases for a consumable like protein powder.
Multiply gross profit per order by lifetime orders: $43 × 2.2 ≈ $95 of lifetime profit in the example.
Deduct acquisition cost incurred only on the first order (about $40 in the example) to see the net profit per acquired customer.
Compare lifetime profit to CAC to sanity-check: source ratio came to 2.3, indicating paid acquisition still makes money over the customer's life.
Be conservative where you have no data — the source treats this as an assumption to revisit, not a fixed truth.
caveats: The 2.2× multiple is an example assumption, not a category benchmark.
Applies best to consumables; one-time-purchase products need a different LTV basis.

cards.title: Sequence the forecast from marketing spend forward
cards.summary: Forecast ecommerce financials by starting with marketing budget, converting it to orders via CAC, then deriving inventory and cash needs.
cards.use_when: You are building a financial model for a new ecommerce or Amazon FBA business and need to know how much inventory and cash to line up.
steps: Start with the marketing budget line by month — the source's example began at $1,000, rose to $1,500, then increased $1,000/month out to month 16.
Apply CAC to convert spend into expected new orders (source example CAC: $41 per order).
Translate orders into units of inventory needed, remembering you must purchase inventory well in advance — the source notes checks of $10,000–$50,000 for stock before any revenue.
Model cash timing explicitly: inventory is paid for before Amazon or customers pay you, so the model must show when cash goes out versus comes in.
Add a cohort/LTV layer to show when paid orders turn profitable through organic sales and repeat purchases.
Use Excel hygiene as the source does: freeze panes on months and cost categories so assumptions stay visible as you build across months.
caveats: The marketing budget trajectory and $41 CAC are source examples, not projections.
Cash timing is the main risk in FBA businesses — the source highlights large upfront inventory payments as the core challenge.

cards.title: Subscription retention benchmarking lesson from Dollar Shave Club
cards.summary: High long-tail retention, not high first-month retention, made a low-AOV subscription valuable.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating or building a low-price subscription and need to understand what makes the model worth investing in.
steps: Look beyond first-month churn: in the Dollar Shave Club cohort cited, roughly 25% of a monthly cohort cancelled within the first month, but retention recovered — about 76% remained one month after signup and around 82% the following month, possibly reflecting pause-and-reactivate features.
Track the long tail: about 51% remained after 10 months, and the second year lost only about 10 percentage points (roughly 51% to 41%), with about 37% still subscribed at 24 months.
Translate retention into revenue: at $5/month, 10 months is $50 and 24 months is $120 per retained customer — the source argues this long tail, not the monthly price, is what produced the valuation.
Apply the lesson to your own subscriber model: small AOV subscriptions can work if the retention curve flattens, which justifies higher acquisition spend.

Also note the source's counterweight: the company grew through low-cost organic/guerrilla marketing because it could not afford ~$50 per paid conversion — a retention story alone did not carry the acquisition.
caveats: The source explicitly warns that very few subscription box businesses see this kind of retention — it is a success story, not a typical outcome.
Cohort data came from a third-party site that scrapes transaction data; treat the exact percentages as estimates.
